keyVerseText: And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
rootMeaning: The Greek adjective ὁλόκληρος (holóklēros) derives from the combination of ὅλος (hólos), meaning 'whole' or 'all,' and κλῆρος (klēros), which can mean 'lot' or 'portion.' This etymology conveys the idea of being 'complete with all that has fallen by lot,' emphasizing fullness and entirety without any part missing. Unlike the simple English glosses 'whole' or 'entire,' the root sense highlights not only completeness but also the inclusion of every part or aspect that belongs, underscoring a perfect and undivided state.
usageInScripture: The term ὁλόκληρος appears only twice in the New Testament, consistently translated as 'whole' or 'entire.' This limited but focused usage shows a consistent emphasis on completeness and perfection, often in a moral or physical sense. The translations reflect the word's nuance of being intact and sound in every part, whether referring to the body, spirit, or other entities, underscoring a holistic integrity.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ὁλόκληρος enriches our grasp of biblical sanctification and spiritual wholeness. It conveys that God desires believers to be sanctified completely—spirit, soul, and body—without division or defect, reflecting the perfect nature of Christ. This completeness is not partial or fragmented but entire, pointing to the transformative power of God’s peace that preserves believers blameless until Christ’s return. It challenges Christians to pursue maturity and integrity in all facets of life, echoing the biblical call to be perfect as our heavenly Father is perfect.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Thessalonians 5:23, the apostle prays that God would sanctify believers 'wholly,' preserving their spirit, soul, and body blameless. The use of ὁλόκληρος here emphasizes a comprehensive sanctification—nothing is left out or neglected. This word deepens the verse’s meaning by portraying sanctification as a complete, undivided work of God’s peace in every dimension of the believer’s being, assuring their readiness for the coming of Jesus Christ.
